description: We’re CHARGE, the aerospace R&D team of İstanbul University-Cerrahpaşa. We build model satellites end to end: flight software, ground stations, electronics and structures, and we placed 8th at the CanSat Competition at PDR stage. We love space missions and turning ideas into working systems. Join a team that has already flown real hardware! We’re looking for teammates with skills in game design, UI/UX, coding, storytelling and space science.
summary: Houston, We Have Failures is a cooperative 2D pixel-art game, built in Godot 4, where 1–4 players launch a spacecraft and keep it alive in orbit. Each player takes a real mission role: Launch & Orbit, Spacecraft Engineer, Communications, or Science Officer. The crew first chooses a rocket. A bigger rocket is more capable but more complex, which sets the difficulty. During launch, every player must time the stage separations together. In orbit, failures appear as timed event cards. The crew must run between four decks to fix them, while tracking power, fuel, memory, thermal and signal levels. Each failure opens a minigame based on a real spacecraft subsystem: power distribution and load shedding, debris avoidance and delta-v, orbit decay and reboost burns, ground station passes, radiation bit flips and parity checks, safe mode, thermal control, reaction wheels, and downlink data budgets. Shared tasks need two roles to coordinate step by step. Every minigame explains its goal, controls and real-world reason, and every fix ends with a fact from real missions. The game turns abstract engineering trade-offs into hands-on teamwork that students can experience, fail at, and learn from.
details:
What it does

Houston, We Have Failures is a cooperative 2D pixel-art game for 1–4 players about running a space mission from launch to operations. Each player takes one role, and the four roles follow the four mission segments from NASA’s mission design resources:

  • Launch & Orbit (launch segment)
  • Spacecraft Engineer (space segment)
  • Communications (ground segment)
  • Science Officer (user segment)
  1. Choose a rocket. Small, medium or large. A bigger rocket is more capable but more complex, and this choice sets the difficulty: how often failures happen and how much time the crew has to fix them.
    • Power line failure: wiring and load shedding
    • Space debris: avoidance burns, inertia and the delta-v budget
    • Orbit decay: drag and reboost burns
    • Ground station pass: tracking a short communication window
    • Radiation bit flip: finding the error with parity bits
    • Solar flare: entering safe mode in the right order
    • Thermal runaway: balancing heaters and radiators in sunlight and shadow
    • Reaction wheel failure: attitude control with momentum
    • Memory almost full: choosing the most valuable data for a limited downlink

Benefits and intended impact

Students rarely get to experience a whole mission or see how one decision affects another. The game makes these trade-offs something you feel: a bigger rocket means more pressure, a wasted burn means less fuel, a missed failure means less mission health. Every minigame opens with a short page explaining its goal, its keys and why it matters in real missions, and every successful fix ends with a real-world fact (for example, how space stations dodge debris and reboost their orbit, or how space telescopes keep working after reaction wheel failures). No prior knowledge is needed, and failing is part of learning.

How it is creative

Instead of a design spreadsheet, the mission becomes a team experience: people running between decks, negotiating who goes where, and holding buttons together. Each minigame simulates the physics or logic of a real system rather than being a generic puzzle; for example, in the debris minigame burns change velocity, not position. The difficulty comes from a real engineering choice, the rocket.

Factors we considered

Accessibility for beginners, readable pixel art and fonts, fair timers based on how long it takes to walk across the ship, solo play (switching between crew members), local multiplayer on one computer with keyboards or gamepads, and keeping every mechanic tied to a real spacecraft concept.

Tools

Godot Engine 4 (GDScript), Pixelorama for our hand-drawn pixel art, the Pixel Operator font (CC0), and Claude (Anthropic) as an AI coding and design assistant.
